summary: Documents the experience gained with BGP-4 between the time it became a Draft Standard and the time it was submitted for Standard. It satisfies the second report requirement of RFC 1264 and augments RFC 1773. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A diary of what people learned while using a routing protocol for years, written to show it was ready for its next step.

questions: how does bgp scale to large networks
subtitle: Lessons learned from years of running BGP-4 in production Internet networks.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 was developed years ago, and it was being elevated from Draft Standard to Internet Standard. The IETF needed to show that it had been successfully deployed and that operators had real experience with it.
tldr.mechanism: This document reports how BGP has been used in production since 1989, covering implementation maturity, operational challenges discovered in real networks, and how certain design choices like metrics and timers work in practice.
tldr.outcome: BGP-4 proved to be stable, widely deployed across 21,000 autonomous systems, carrying over 170,000 routes. However, operational experience revealed design considerations about how different vendors implement optional features and edge cases.

facts.label: Autonomous systems at time of writing

today: RFC 4277 is Informational and documents BGP-4's successful deployment. BGP remains the Internet's inter-domain routing protocol and is used across all autonomous systems on the Internet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document explains how BGP-4 has met the IETF's requirements for advancing from Draft Standard to Internet Standard. The IETF standards process requires that before a protocol achieves Standard status, there must be evidence that it is well understood, stable, and successfully deployed. This memo documents that BGP-4 meets these criteria.

BGP-4 had been in production use since 1993, and BGP itself even longer (since 1989), so there was years of operational data to draw from. This document augments an earlier report (RFC 1773) by describing additional knowledge gained while the protocol was at Draft Standard status.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a rule becomes official, people need to prove it actually works in the real world. This memo shows that BGP-4 has been running the Internet's routing for years without major problems.

sections.title: How BGP-4 Works in Real Networks
sections.content:
At the time of writing, BGP-4 was deployed as the inter-autonomous system routing protocol between all Internet-attached autonomous systems. The Internet had nearly 21,000 active autonomous systems, and BGP routers were carrying over 170,000 aggregate route entries, representing several times that many connected networks. Some core routers had more than 2.5 million active paths in their routing tables.

BGP runs over diverse hardware: from slow general-purpose CPUs to high-performance RISC network processors, on both special-purpose routers and workstations running various Unix and other operating systems. Links range from 56 Kbps to 10 Gbps. BGP systems exchange routing information between stub autonomous systems and transit networks, and between multiple transit providers. There is no protocol distinction between so-called backbone networks and edge networks.

AS path lengths are typically around 10 hops for native paths, though some networks show padded paths of 25 or more autonomous systems. BGP peering is used both for the exchange of routing information between a transit provider and a stub customer, and between multiple transit providers.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP runs on routers big and small, on fast links and slow links, all over the world. When this was written, it was connecting 21,000 different networks and carrying information about hundreds of thousands of routes.

sections.title: Metrics, Policies, and Design Choices
sections.content:
BGP uses two different metric systems: MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) for inter-domain routing (comparing multiple paths from different external peers) and LOCAL_PREF for intra-domain routing (comparing paths within a single autonomous system). This separation allows each autonomous system to define independent policies for traffic entering and leaving the network.

Operational experience revealed that MED values are often derived from internal routing metrics, which can cause problems when comparing MEDs across different autonomous systems that use different internal protocols or metric spaces. The document notes that many implementations provide the capability to compare MEDs between different autonomous systems, even though the spec intended MEDs to be compared only between paths from the same peer AS.

Other operational lessons include the importance of controlling message packing (how many routes go in each UPDATE message), rate limiting updates to manage network load, and ordering of path attributes for compatibility with different implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP uses point scores to pick the best path. Operational experience showed some tricks vendors use with those scores can cause surprises, and there are careful decisions about how fast to send updates to avoid overwhelming the network.

sections.title: Scaling BGP in Large Networks
sections.content:
The original BGP design required each internal BGP router to maintain a connection to every other internal BGP router (a full-mesh topology). This approach does not scale to networks with many routers. Operational experience led to two main techniques for scaling internal BGP: Route Reflection (initially RFC 1966, updated to RFC 2796) and Autonomous System Confederations (initially RFC 1965, updated to RFC 3065). These techniques allow networks to avoid full-mesh connections while still exchanging routing information reliably.

Many networks use a mix of both techniques. This operational experience drove the development of these extensions, making BGP practical for very large networks.
sections.plainLanguage: If every router has to talk to every other router, that becomes impossible with hundreds of routers. People invented tricks to let routers delegate and pass messages along instead, which BGP now supports.

sections.title: Security and Operational Robustness
sections.content:
The primary security mechanism for BGP is the TCP MD5 Signature Option (RFC 2385), which provides authentication that BGP messages come from a known peer. This helps prevent accidental misconfiguration and some categories of attacks, though it does not prevent a distant attacker from injecting false routes.

Other possible mechanisms like IPsec (RFC 2401) and TLS (RFC 2246) were rarely or never used in BGP deployments at the time. The document notes that BGP is inherently vulnerable to false route advertisements from autonomous systems more than one hop away, but no transmission security mechanism can address this threat; that would require schemes like S-BGP that include cryptographic path validation.

The document also discusses the BGP finite state machine for managing the connection lifecycle, the handling of TCP characteristics that BGP must adapt to, and the operational considerations for timers and hold time configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP uses a secret shared between two routers to prove messages are real, protecting against nearby attackers and mistakes. But a sneaky router far away could still lie about routes to networks.
